'''Peter Goldreich''' (born July 14, 1939) is an American [[astrophysics|astrophysicist]] whose research focuses on [[celestial mechanics]], planetary rings, [[helioseismology]] and [[neutron star]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.astro.caltech.edu/department/bluebook/goldreich.html|title = Caltech Astronomy : Peter Goldreich's Research Interests|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060912125405/http://www.astro.caltech.edu/department/bluebook/goldreich.html|archive-date = 2006-09-12}}</ref>  He is the Lee DuBridge Professor of Astrophysics and Planetary Physics at [[California Institute of Technology]].  Since 2005 he has also been a professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.france-science.org/home/page.asp?target=news&ID=848|title = L'Académie des Sciences remet la Grande Médaille 2006 à l'astrophysicien américain Peter Goldreich|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071027170554/http://www.france-science.org/home/page.asp?target=news&ID=848|archive-date = 2007-10-27}}</ref><ref name="IASLETTER"/>  Asteroid [[3805 Goldreich]] is named after him.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://scully.cfa.harvard.edu/~cgi/ShowCitation.COM?num=3805 |title=Citation for (3805) |publisher=Minor Planet Center |access-date=2007-12-14 |archive-date=2018-05-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180509012546/http://scully.cfa.harvard.edu/~cgi/ShowCitation.COM?num=3805 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
Goldreich received a bachelor of science in engineering physics from [[Cornell University]] in 1960, and obtained a Ph.D. from Cornell in 1963 under the supervision of [[Thomas Gold]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ias.edu/about/faculty-and-emeriti/goldreich|title = Institute for Advanced Study: Faculty and Emeriti: Goldreich|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120716224000/http://www.ias.edu/people/faculty-and-emeriti/goldreich|archive-date = 2012-07-16}}</ref><ref name = "SELF">{{cite web|url = http://www.sns.ias.edu/~pmg/|title = Peter Goldreich}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://intl.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/short/305/5680/39b?ck=nck |title=Random Samples |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930225101/http://intl.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/short/305/5680/39b?ck=nck |archive-date=2007-09-30 }}</ref><ref name="PMAAWRDS">{{cite web|url = http://www.pma.caltech.edu/GSR/pmahonors.html|title = PMA Division News Honors & Awards|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120207055801/http://www.pma.caltech.edu/GSR/pmahonors.html|archive-date = 2012-02-07}}</ref>  In 1963 and 1964 Goldreich was a postdoctoral fellow at [[Cambridge University]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.bibalex.org/Eclipse2006/FrontiersSpeakers/Peter%20Goldreich.htm|title = Prof. Peter Goldreich: Lee A. DuBridge Professor of Astrophysics & Planetary Physics, Caltech}}</ref>   From 1964 to 1966 he was an [[assistant professor]] of astronomy and geophysics at [[UCLA]].  Goldreich joined the faculty at [[Caltech]] in 1966 as an [[associate professor]].<ref name = "SELF" /><ref name = "awardarchive">{{cite web|url = http://today.caltech.edu/today/story-archive?section_id=11226|title = Archives for Honors and Awards}}</ref>  He later became a full [[professor]] in 1969 while remaining at Caltech, and in 1981 he became the [[Lee Alvin DuBridge|Lee A. DuBridge Professor of Astrophysics & Planetary Physics]] also at Caltech.<ref name = "SELF" />  He also sits on the Board of Adjudicators for the [[Shaw Prize]], and the selection committee for Astronomy Prizes.

==Scientific accomplishments==
Goldreich has made a wide range of significant contributions to theoretical astrophysics and planetary sciences. In 1966 Goldreich published a classic paper on the evolution of [[Orbit of the Moon|the Moon's orbit]] and on the orbits of other moons in the Solar System.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Peter Goldreich|title=History of the Lunar Orbit|journal=[[Reviews of Geophysics]]|volume=4|issue=4|pages=411–439|date=Nov 1966|doi=10.1029/RG004i004p00411|bibcode=1966RvGSP...4..411G}} Termed "classic" by {{cite journal|last1=[[Jihad Touma]] & [[Jack Wisdom]]|title=Evolution of the Earth-Moon system|journal=[[The Astronomical Journal]]|volume=108|pages=1943|date=Nov 1994|doi=10.1086/117209|bibcode=1994AJ....108.1943T|doi-access=free}}</ref> He showed that for each planet there is a certain distance such that moons closer to the planet than that distance maintain an almost constant orbital inclination with respect to the planet's equator (with an [[Nodal precession|orbital precession]] mostly due to the tidal influence of the planet), whereas moons further away maintain an almost constant orbital inclination with respect to the [[ecliptic]] (with precession due mostly to the tidal influence of the Sun). The moons in the first category, with the exception of [[Neptune]]'s moon [[Triton (moon)|Triton]], orbit near the equatorial plane. He concluded that these moons formed from equatorial [[accretion disk]]s. But he found that the Moon, although it was once inside the critical distance from the Earth, never had an equatorial orbit as would be expected from various scenarios for its origin. This is called the lunar inclination problem, to which various solutions have since been proposed.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kaveh Pahlevan & Alessandro Morbidelli|title=Collisionless encounters and the origin of the lunar inclination|journal=Nature|volume=527|issue=7579|pages=492–494|date=Nov 26, 2015|doi=10.1038/nature16137|pmid=26607544|arxiv=1603.06515|bibcode=2015Natur.527..492P|s2cid=4456736}}</ref>

Goldreich and [[Alar Toomre]] first described the process of [[polar wander]] in a 1969 paper, although evidence of [[paleomagnetism]] was not discovered until later.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Did the Dinosaurs Live on a Topsy-Turvy Earth?|journal = Science|volume = 287|issue = 5452|pages = 406–407|doi = 10.1126/science.287.5452.406|year = 2000|last1 = Kerr|first1 = R. A.|s2cid = 129200632}}</ref> Goldreich collaborated with [[George Ogden Abell|George Abell]] to conclude that [[planetary nebulae]] evolved from [[red giant]] stars, a view that is now widely accepted.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://content.cdlib.org/xtf/view?docId=hb4d5nb20m&doc.view=content&chunk.id=div00002&toc.depth=1&brand=calisphere&anchor.id=0|title = University of California: In Memoriam, 1985}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://parked.ihwy.com/~barbour/jeff/books/Stars_by_Night/march_2006.html |title=The Stars by Night and Day |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071008052228/http://parked.ihwy.com/~barbour/jeff/books/Stars_by_Night/march_2006.html |archive-date=2007-10-08 }}</ref>  In 1979 Goldreich, along with [[Scott Tremaine]] predicted that [[Saturn]]'s F ring was maintained by [[shepherd moon]]s, a prediction that would be confirmed by observations in 1980.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.solarviews.com/eng/saturnbg.htm|title = Historical Background of Saturn's Rings}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.cfm?release=2002-190|title = Chaos Seen in Movement of Ring-Herding Moons of Saturn|website = [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]]|access-date = 2007-05-11|archive-date = 2016-01-15|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160115062149/http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?release=2002-190|url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url = http://partners.nytimes.com/library/national/science/062789sci-nasa-saturn.html|title = New Clues Emerge in Mystery of Planetary Rings | work=The New York Times | date=December 8, 1999 | access-date=May 22, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url = https://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1511/is_v7/ai_5083814|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20050411150531/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1511/is_v7/ai_5083814|url-status = usurped|archive-date = April 11, 2005|work = Discover (magazine)|volume = 7|title = Voyager was on target again; in the latest unmanned triumph, Voyager 2 surveyed Uranus and sent back a real bull's-eye}} </ref>  They also predicted that [[Uranus]]' rings were held in place by similar shepherd moons, a prediction that was confirmed in 1986.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://ciar.ca/web/home.nsf/pages/home.0380|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071011062904/http://www.ciar.ca/web/home.nsf/pages/home.0380|url-status = dead|archive-date = 2007-10-11|title = Cosmologist Scott Tremaine receives two honors}}</ref>  Goldreich, along with Tremaine predicted planetary migration in 1980, which would later be invoked to explain [[hot jupiter]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://media4.obspm.fr/exoplanets/pages_histoire/trois-premieres.html|title = The three first giant exoplanets|access-date = 2007-05-11|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130219164036/http://media4.obspm.fr/exoplanets/pages_histoire/trois-premieres.html|archive-date = 2013-02-19|url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://abob.libs.uga.edu/bobk/ccc/cc083199.html |title=PLUTO, KBOs AND A NEW THEORY OF PLANETARY FORMATION |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060901094822/http://abob.libs.uga.edu/bobk/ccc/cc083199.html |archive-date=2006-09-01 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://intl.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/full/276/5317/1336?ck=nck |title=Worlds Around Other Stars Shake Planet Birth Theory |journal=Science |volume=276 |issue=5317 |pages=1336–1339 |bibcode=1997Sci...276.1336G |last1=Glanz |first1=J. |year=1997 |doi=10.1126/science.276.5317.1336 |s2cid=119044504 |url-access=subscription }}{{dead link|date=May 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 1969, Goldreich published a paper<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goldreich |first1=Peter |last2=Julian |first2=William |title=Pulsar electrodynamics |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=157 |pages=869 |date=1969 |bibcode=1969ApJ...157..869G |doi=10.1086/150119 }}</ref> together with William Julian that is now considered a classic work on pulsar magnetospheres. They provided a simple and compelling model for the structure of magnetic fields anchored in a neutron star and showed that these fields can extract the neutron star rotational energy to power electromagnetic emission. Similar considerations were later used to understand the magnetospheres of rotating black holes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blandford |first1=Roger |last2=Znajek |first2=Roman |title=Electromagnetic extraction of energy from Kerr black holes |journal=MNRAS |volume=179 |issue=3 |pages=433–456 |date=1977 |bibcode=1977MNRAS.179..433B |doi=10.1093/mnras/179.3.433 |doi-access=free |arxiv=astro-ph/0506302 }}</ref>

In 1995, Goldreich received the [[National Medal of Science]] for "his profound and lasting contributions to planetary sciences and astrophysics, providing fundamental theoretical insights for understanding the rotation of planets, the dynamics of planetary rings, pulsars, astrophysical masers, the spiral arms of galaxies, and the oscillations of the Sun".<ref name = "ORIGINS" /><ref name = "IASLETTER"/><ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=141|title = The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121003064422/http://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=141|archive-date = 2012-10-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.jinfo.org/Medal_of_Science.html|title = JEWISH RECIPIENTS OF THE US NATIONAL MEDAL OF SCIENCE|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121027101811/http://www.jinfo.org/Medal_of_Science.html|archive-date = 2012-10-27}}</ref>

Goldreich was awarded the [[Grande Médaille]] of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 2006 for his numerous contributions in the field of Astrophysics.<ref name = "PMAAWRDS" /><ref name = "awardarchive" /><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.france-science.org/home/page.asp?target=news&ID=850|title = French Academy of Science awards Grand Medal to astrophysicist Peter Goldreich|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071027170536/http://www.france-science.org/home/page.asp?target=news&ID=850|archive-date = 2007-10-27}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://autonomy.caltech.edu/autonomy/TierscalablePress/Archives%20for%20Honors%20and%20Awards.pdf|title = Archives for Honors and Awards|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081031140526/http://autonomy.caltech.edu/autonomy/TierscalablePress/Archives%20for%20Honors%20and%20Awards.pdf|archive-date = 2008-10-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/06Fall/|title = Institute for Advanced Study: The Institute Letter|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071030071342/http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/06Fall/|archive-date = 2007-10-30}}</ref>

Goldreich received the 2007 [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy "in recognition of his lifetime achievements in theoretical astrophysics and planetary sciences".<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.shawprize.org/en/laureates/2007/astronomy/Goldreich/release.html|title = The Shaw Prize – Peter Goldreich – Announcement and Citation|access-date = 2007-06-14|archive-date = 2008-09-08|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080908012534/http://www.shawprize.org/en/laureates/2007/astronomy/Goldreich/release.html|url-status = dead}}</ref>
